content.overview: Specialist instruction for sanitation deviations, verification, capa & handoff in propagation and clean-stock operations.

sections.title: Record what was observed and what control failed
sections.body: A deviation record should identify the expected control, observed departure, affected material/area, immediate containment, evidence preserved and responsible follow-up. It should not invent a root cause before investigation.

sections.title: Verification is evidence that the process occurred
sections.body: Completed checklists, tool-change logs, area-release records and traceable sanitation steps can verify execution. Verification of execution is different from proving pathogen eradication.

sections.title: Corrective action should target the demonstrated failure mode
sections.body: When evidence supports a workflow weakness, corrective action can address training, layout, sequencing, labeling or process controls. Effectiveness requires follow-up evidence rather than a closed form alone.

commonMistakes: Writing a root cause before evidence supports it.
Treating a completed sanitation checklist as proof that all biological risk is eliminated.
Closing a deviation without an accountable follow-up or effectiveness check.
content.practicalApplication: Build a biosecurity deviation and handoff record from a simulated propagation breach, separating observation, containment, investigation question, corrective action owner and effectiveness evidence.
content.summary: Strong biosecurity records preserve what happened, what was controlled, what remains uncertain and who owns the next decision.
